site.name: Alpine Tunnel East Portal & Railroad Grade
site.location: Alpine Tunnel Historic District / Hancock approach
overview: The Alpine Tunnel was the centerpiece of a Denver, South Park and Pacific Railroad route across the Continental Divide, linking the eastern approach from Hancock with the western approach toward Quartz.
The National Register-listed historic district preserves the railroad grade and associated features across roughly 13 miles, while the tunnel itself extends 1,772 feet beneath the divide.

timeline.text: Construction crews built the high-elevation railroad approach and excavated the Alpine Tunnel beneath the Continental Divide.
The Denver, South Park and Pacific and successor railroads used the Alpine Tunnel route as part of their mountain transportation network.
Railroad use of the Alpine Tunnel route ended after roughly three decades of operation.
The Alpine Tunnel, railroad grade, station area, and related resources were recognized together as the Alpine Tunnel Historic District.

moreHistory: National Register documentation describes the Alpine Tunnel Historic District as 13.3 contiguous miles following the former Denver, South Park and Pacific Railroad right-of-way across Chaffee and Gunnison counties.

The tunnel runs 1,772 feet beneath Altman Pass. Its eastern approach curves inside the portal before the bore continues toward the Continental Divide; the tunnel was built with a slight grade to provide drainage toward both portals.

The historic district includes much more than the bore itself, preserving the railbed and associated railroad landscape. This Remnant entry focuses on the Chaffee County east-portal and railroad-grade side of that larger district.

Historic documentation records substantial collapse within the tunnel, including a section that sealed the eastern portal. The location should be understood as a historic railroad landscape rather than an invitation to enter underground workings.
